question.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)={e}^{3x}$ and the denominator $v(x)={x}^{3}+1.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=3{e}^{3x},\,{v}^{′}(x)=3{x}^{2}.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3{e}^{3x})({x}^{3}+1)-({e}^{3x})(3{x}^{2})}{({x}^{3}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3({x}^{3}+1){e}^{3x}-3{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}}{({x}^{3}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3(({x}^{3}+1)-{x}^{2}){e}^{3x}}{({x}^{3}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+1){e}^{3x}}{{({x}^{3}+1)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
